artifacts.summary: Trap-driven terminal record, result subcommand with expect-pid/expect-scope assertions, STATUS line, and full documentation; 47/47 suite passing.

completion_data.completion_summary: Made lake-build-guard.sh's on-disk build record terminal on every trappable exit path (including a discovered pre-existing bug where any failing build skipped finalize_record entirely) and added a result subcommand exposing the build verdict through the guard's own exit code, with --expect-pid/--expect-scope ownership assertions and a belt-and-braces STATUS stderr line; test suite grew from 29 to 47 passing checks, shellcheck clean, no task-number references.

memory_candidates.content: Bash pitfall found in lake-build-guard.sh: a function that reactivates `set -e` internally (e.g. `set +e; cmd; rc=$?; set -e`) before its own tail `return "$rc"` will trigger errexit-driven premature script termination whenever rc is nonzero, even though the CALLER already wrapped the call in its own `set +e ... set -e` bracket -- `set -e`/`set +e` are global shell options, not scoped per call frame, so a nested re-enable leaks back into that same function's own remaining statements including its own return. Fix: never reactivate `set -e` immediately before a `return` that might carry a nonzero value; let the caller restore it only after safely capturing the return value.

For a bash EXIT/INT/TERM trap meant to finalize idempotent cleanup state (e.g. a terminal record on a build guard), use a single GLOBAL (never `local`) idempotency flag checked/set at the very top of the trap handler, plus explicit `trap - EXIT INT TERM` after the normal cleanup path -- both together, since either alone is insufficient (a `local` flag is fragile across dynamic-scoping/signal-delivery boundaries; clearing the trap alone doesn't help if a later code path re-arms it). When testing a killed-holder path under `setsid`, read the process's own recorded PID from its own output/state (not bash's `$!`) as the process-group handle for `kill -TERM -- -$pgid`, since `setsid`'s fork behavior is ambiguous depending on the calling shell's own process-group/job-control state.
